raw_case_text:
A 53-year-old morbidly obese female with a history of hypertension presented to the emergency department (ED), with a sudden onset of loss of consciousness, left-sided weakness, and altered sensorium for two days, which was associated with high-grade fever and vomiting. At admission, she was unconscious (Glasgow coma scale, or GCS, score = 5); had tachypnea (respiratory rate, or RR, 30-35 minute-1), tachycardia (heart rate, or HR, 114 bpm), and blood pressure (BP) 153/90 mmHg; was maintaining oxygen saturation of 94% to 94% (on room air) on spontaneous respiration; and was passing urine output around 40-50 mL/hour. Given airway protection, tracheal intubation was performed immediately. Post intubation, the GCS was 6. Noncontrast computerized tomography (NCCT) of the brain revealed right basal ganglia bleeding with intraventricular hemorrhage (Figure 1).
Then she was transferred to ICU, where cerebral protection strategy (head-up position, neck in a neutral position, osmotic diuretics, mean arterial pressure (MAP) 85-90 mm Hg, normoxia, normocarbia, euglycemia, normothermia, and maintenance of sodium (Na+) levels between 145 and 155 mEq/L) and further supportive care was initiated. Laboratory evaluation at admission is summarized in Table 1. Electrocardiography (ECG) showed sinus tachycardia. Chest X-ray (CXR) was normal.   
After a few days of ICU admission, she started spiking high-grade temperature (core temperature as high as 106-107  F), which was associated with rhabdomyolysis (serum creatine kinase (CK-total) = 10,000 IU/L), stage III acute kidney injury (AKI, requiring five sessions of renal replacement therapy), and coagulopathy (requiring blood component therapy). On workup, cultures turned out to be sterile. Other possibilities of hyperthermia (such as drug toxicity) were ruled out. NCCT head was repeated, which did not reveal any hematoma expansion. Workup for COVID-19 was also negative. On account of a history of fever with chill and myalgia around a week before ED admission, a tropical workup was sent for malaria, typhoid, leptospirosis, dengue, chikungunya, and scrub typhus, in which serology (IgM antibodies) for dengue turned out to be positive. Gradually, the temperature trends, renal functions, and coagulopathy recovered. In intercurrent issues, she had septic shock (secondary to ventilator-associated pneumonia and grade IV pressure injury in the sacral region) and neuromuscular weakness, resulting in prolonged weaning. Eventually, the patient was discharged after six months of ICU stay in tracheostomized condition, with a GCS score of 9, accepting Ryle's tube feeding and passing adequate urine output.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 53-year-old morbidly obese female presented with a 2-day history of sudden-onset loss of consciousness, left-sided weakness, altered sensorium, high-grade fever, and vomiting.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Approximately 1 week prior to emergency department admission, the patient experienced fever with chills and myalgia. Two days prior to admission, she developed a sudden onset of loss of consciousness, left-sided weakness, and altered sensorium accompanied by high-grade fever and vomiting. After admission and ICU transfer for a right basal ganglia intracerebral hemorrhage, she developed extreme hyperthermia (core temperature 106-107 F), severe rhabdomyolysis, stage III acute kidney injury, and coagulopathy.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for preceding fever with chills and myalgia (1 week prior), followed by high-grade fever, vomiting, left-sided weakness, and loss of consciousness.

objective.physical_examination: On admission: unconscious with a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 5 (improving to GCS 6 immediately post-intubation), left-sided weakness, tachypnea (respiratory rate 30-35/min), tachycardia (heart rate 114 bpm), blood pressure 153/90 mm Hg, SpO2 94% on room air, and urine output 40-50 mL/hour. In ICU: spiked core temperatures of 106-107 F and later developed a grade IV sacral pressure ulcer and ICU neuromuscular weakness.
objective.routine_investigations: ECG: sinus tachycardia. Chest X-ray: normal. ICU laboratory evolution: severe rhabdomyolysis with total serum creatine kinase (CK) 10,000 IU/L, stage III acute kidney injury, and coagulopathy. Microbiological cultures: sterile. COVID-19 testing: negative. Tropical fever panel (malaria, typhoid, leptospirosis, dengue, chikungunya, and scrub typhus): positive for dengue IgM antibodies and negative for chikungunya and other tropical pathogens.
objective.advanced_workup: Admission noncontrast brain CT (NCCT): right basal ganglia intracerebral hemorrhage with intraventricular hemorrhage. Repeat head NCCT (during extreme hyperthermia workup): no hematoma expansion.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Acute dengue fever complicated by spontaneous right basal ganglia intracerebral and intraventricular hemorrhage, central/infectious extreme hyperthermia (106-107 F), severe rhabdomyolysis, stage III acute kidney injury, and coagulopathy. Bacterial sepsis at admission, COVID-19, malaria, typhoid, leptospirosis, chikungunya, scrub typhus, and drug-induced hyperthermia were excluded. Confirmation: Positive serum dengue IgM serology and head NCCT demonstrating right basal ganglia and intraventricular hemorrhage. Management and outcome: Immediately intubated for airway protection and managed in the ICU with neuroprotective measures (head-of-bed elevation, osmotic diuretics, MAP target 85-90 mm Hg, hyperosmolar sodium target 145-155 mEq/L, temperature/glycemic control), five sessions of renal replacement therapy for AKI, and blood component transfusions for coagulopathy. Hyperthermia, renal function, and coagulopathy resolved, though her prolonged 6-month ICU course was complicated by ventilator-associated pneumonia with septic shock, a grade IV sacral pressure injury, and critical illness neuromuscular weakness; she was ultimately discharged tracheostomized with a GCS of 9 on Ryle's tube feeding and adequate spontaneous diuresis.
